As vibe coding — using AI prompts to write programs — becomes increasingly popular, the number of new apps submitted to the App Store has surged, doubling in the first half of 2026 — yet downloads have grown by just 2%. Here's a full roundup.

New app submissions soar, but downloads lag far behind

The New York Times published a report today, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, noting that while the number of new apps submitted to the App Store in the first half of 2026 doubled, downloads rose by only 2%.

The report also highlights two developers who have been consistently releasing vibe-coded apps on the App Store: Marco Pérez plans to quit his job at JPMorgan next month to develop apps full-time; David Svensson has launched 11 niche apps over the past five months, treating vibe coding as a hobby rather than a business.

Excerpts from the report are as follows:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago, had never developed a mobile app before. He spent five weeks over the winter researching "vibe coding" AI tools to build a prototype, then another two weeks preparing it for App Store submission. His app InfoDrizzle performed reasonably well, accumulating 1,300 downloads to date and earning roughly $500 in profit. Pérez's next app was even more popular. He spent about a week in May launching Stampa, a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital postage stamps, which has since recorded 20,000 downloads and generated around $3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian told the New York Times of another issue arising from the surge in submissions: the App Store's review process has come under enormous pressure, as earlier reports have noted.

Ajemian said, "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," and added that Apple "welcomes a new generation of developers building and launching apps at an unprecedented pace using the latest tools."

He also noted that all apps "must meet the same high standards of quality, privacy, and safety that users have always relied on, whether they are developed through vibe coding or not."
